newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Habsburg visits assassination site in Sarajevo.
newsitem.headline: Habsburg visits assassination site in Sarajevo.

text.p: A descendant of the Habsburg monarchy recalled his grandfather's assassination in a visit to the Bosnian capital Sarajevo on Sunday, saying it was time to heal the wounds of a violent century.

Otto von Habsburg, 84, the oldest living member of the Austrian royal family, laid flowers and prayed at the street corner where Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife were shot in 1914 in an assassination that sparked World War One.
"When we stood on the bridge where Franz Ferdinand was killed we were aware what a great influence that event had on the future of Europe," Habsburg told reporters afterward.
"With that event, the epoch of war in Europe began. That event was not only the cause of war but the beginning of all the tragedies which followed and the opening of the path to Auschwitz.
"The tragedies which started at that place should be stopped there too," he said.
In his first visit to the city, Habsburg said he did not wish to dwell on his family's history and said he wanted to help Bosnia forge ties to the European Union after a devastating war.
Habsburg, who led a delegation from the Pan-European Union, held talks with Moslem and Croat members of the country's peacetime presidency on Saturday.
He said Europe's future would be decided by efforts at building reconciliation among rival Moslem, Roman Catholic Croat and Orthodox Serb communities in Bosnia.
"If we succeed to provide co-existence for all religions and nations in this town, we will succeed to do this in the whole world -- not just in Europe."
As a member of a family that presided over the former Austro-Hungarian empire, Habsburg said he had inherited a keen interest in Bosnia.
"Sarajevo was a reality for me even I was two years old. It is clear that in a family which is politically oriented towards Bosnia that Sarajevo remains in the genes," he said.
After annexing Bosnia in 1878, the Austro-Hungarian empire ruled Bosnia until World War One.
The old communist-ruled Yugoslav federation portrayed the Bosnian Serb who shot Franz Ferdinand as a hero fighting imperialist oppressors.
The Sarajevo street where the archduke was shot was named after the assassin, Gavrilo Princip. A plaque and footprints in the pavement honoured his memory.
After Bosnia seceded from Serbian-led Yugoslavia in 1992, the mainly Moslem and Croat authorities in Sarajevo removed the plaque and footprints and renamed the street.
